item.title: Daily Gaming & Tech Brief — September 17, 2026
item.description:
1. GAME & TECH NEWS

GAME NEWS

1) September's release calendar is entering its busiest stretch

The second half of September is bringing a dense sequence of PC releases, Early Access launches and major updates. Steam's current release calendar includes Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter, The Guild 1 Remake: Europa 1410, Kernel Hearts and several smaller releases on September 17, followed by Dressmaker, Graveyard Keeper 2 and other launches over the following days. The schedule then builds toward Silent Hill: Townfall, CONTROL Resonant, Nivalis Nights and Minecraft Dungeons 2 later in the month, giving the autumn PC season a particularly crowded storefront. For players, the important change is not one single blockbuster but the number of games competing for attention at the same time.

2) Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter arrives on Steam

The second chapter of the Trails in the Sky remake project has reached Steam as part of the current September RPG wave. Its arrival is significant for PC players following Nihon Falcom's long-running Trails series because it continues a modernized presentation of one of the franchise's earlier story arcs while keeping the connected, character-driven structure that defines the series. The launch also lands during Steam's Party-Based RPG Fest, putting it in front of an audience already browsing turn-based and party-focused RPGs.

3) The Guild 1 Remake: Europa 1410 enters Early Access

The Guild 1 Remake: Europa 1410 is joining Steam's Early Access lineup, bringing its medieval life-simulation and strategy formula back into the spotlight. The game combines character progression, business management, social systems and political maneuvering rather than focusing only on conventional combat. Its Early Access launch means the development process will continue after release, with feedback and future updates expected to shape the final version. It is one of several management and simulation games arriving during a very crowded September schedule.

4) Steam's Party-Based RPG Fest is filling the storefront with demos and discounts

Steam's Party-Based RPG Fest is running from September 14 through September 21 and focuses on games built around controllable groups of characters with different roles, equipment and abilities. The event mixes released games with upcoming titles and demos, so it is more than a conventional discount period. Developers are using the festival to launch character trailers, announce participation and run temporary discounts, while established RPGs receive storefront visibility alongside smaller projects. The event is particularly relevant this week because several new party-based games are launching around the same period.

5) EA and Savvy Games are back in focus after the huge EA transaction

Reporting around Electronic Arts and Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group has put another possible major consolidation in the games industry under attention. The Public Investment Fund's acquisition of EA was reported at roughly $55 billion, and subsequent reporting has discussed the possibility of combining EA's major properties with Savvy's broader games portfolio. A potential combination would bring together franchises and businesses spanning sports, shooters, life simulation and mobile games, although any further transaction remains subject to corporate decisions and regulatory considerations. The story is part of a much larger restructuring of the games industry following several years of acquisitions, layoffs and changing investment strategies.

TECH NEWS

1) Huawei says demand for its Ascend AI processors is exceeding supply

Huawei chairman Eric Xu said demand for the company's Ascend AI hardware is already exceeding production capacity in China. The company is also preparing newer Ascend processors and developing larger-scale interconnect technology intended to combine very large numbers of processors into a single computing system. The strategy reflects the pressure created by restrictions on access to some leading U.S. AI accelerators and software ecosystems. Rather than relying on a single chip to close the performance gap, Huawei is increasingly emphasizing system-level scaling and domestic infrastructure.

2) Apple is considering enterprise AI servers based on its own silicon

Reuters has reported that Apple is exploring enterprise-oriented AI servers built around its custom silicon, with Nvidia interconnect technology also reportedly being considered. The project is described as an inference-focused effort with a possible long-term target rather than a confirmed product launch, so specifications and timing could still change substantially. If pursued, it would extend Apple's custom-chip strategy beyond phones, Macs and tablets into large-scale data-center infrastructure. It would also put Apple into a market where Nvidia, AMD and specialized accelerator companies currently dominate.

3) GNOME 51 launches with major graphics and performance changes

GNOME 51 has released with improvements aimed at frame scheduling, screen capture, monitor settings and the desktop graphics stack. The release also removes reliance on older Nvidia driver interfaces, continuing the project's move toward newer Linux graphics infrastructure. For gaming and media users, the practical areas to watch are smoother frame delivery and faster capture rather than a single headline feature. Distribution maintainers still need to package the release, so users on rolling and fixed-release distributions will receive it at different times.

4) Snap is targeting enterprise use for its Specs AR glasses

Snap is positioning its new Specs augmented-reality glasses as an enterprise product, with partnerships involving Salesforce, Nvidia and AWS. The glasses are intended for use cases such as field service, retail and industrial workflows, where hands-free information and visual guidance can have a direct business purpose. Pricing is in the thousands of dollars rather than consumer-gadget territory, which makes the product's success dependent on whether companies can justify the hardware through measurable productivity gains. The strategy puts Snap into a growing enterprise AR market alongside other major headset and smart-glasses platforms.

5) Linux gaming infrastructure continues to expand beyond traditional x86 PCs

Valve's work around Steam Frame is drawing attention to compatibility layers such as FEX and Lepton, which are designed to let software built for different architectures and operating environments work on the device. The broader significance is that Linux gaming compatibility is increasingly becoming a multi-architecture problem rather than simply a Windows-to-x86 Linux problem. Android application support and translation layers add another compatibility target alongside Wine, Proton and traditional Linux binaries. That work could influence how future SteamOS hardware handles software that was never designed specifically for its underlying architecture.

2. STEAM SALE / EVENT

Steam Party-Based RPG Fest — September 14–21

Steam's Party-Based RPG Fest is the main current Steam-wide genre event, running from September 14 through September 21. The festival focuses on RPGs where players build and manage a party of multiple characters, with individual roles, equipment, abilities and progression. The event includes discounts, demos and upcoming games, giving smaller projects a chance to appear alongside established RPGs. Developers participating in the event are also using the week for character showcases, new announcements and temporary discounts, while older titles receive large reductions across individual games and bundles.

The event is particularly active because it overlaps with several current RPG releases. Steam's own upcoming-release listings show Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter and other party-oriented games arriving during the same period, while individual developers are advertising their participation and event discounts. The result is a festival that functions as both a sale and a discovery event rather than simply a storefront coupon period.

3. XODUS

Current status

Xodus remains an active open-source project focused on bringing Xbox PC and Game Pass software to Linux and macOS. Its architecture covers account authentication, content acquisition, Xbox runtime compatibility, packaged-game handling and integration with Wine-based execution. The project has moved beyond the idea of being only a launcher because its public work is concerned with the layers required between obtaining a game and actually making its Windows-specific runtime behave correctly on another operating system.

1) Authentication and account-related components are already documented as working pieces of the project, giving Xodus a functional foundation rather than leaving it at a graphical frontend stage.

2) Xbox runtime compatibility remains a major area of development because Xbox PC titles can depend on Microsoft runtime components that ordinary Windows games do not require.

3) MSIXVC packaging and newer Xbox content formats remain important engineering targets, since the way Microsoft packages and distributes these games directly affects what a third-party Linux client has to understand.

4) The project has documented execution of some backward-compatible Xbox titles, while broader modern-game support depends on additional compatibility work and game-specific requirements.

Progress: active development toward game execution

4. FREE GAMES

Epic Games Store

Astral Ascent and Luftrausers are the current Epic Games Store free-to-keep games for the September 10–17 window. Astral Ascent is a 2D platforming roguelite with four playable heroes and local co-op support, while Luftrausers is a retro-inspired arcade shooter built around high-score runs and aerial combat. Both remain in the player's Epic library after being claimed during the promotion. The next scheduled giveaway window, beginning September 17, is Mindcop and Shogun Showdown.

Amazon Prime / Luna

The September 17 Prime Gaming drop includes DOOM Eternal through a Microsoft Store code, Rims Racing through Epic Games Store and Wall World 2 through the Amazon Games App. These are claimable games rather than temporary free weekends, with redemption tied to the specified storefront or service. Prime's next scheduled wave adds further titles on September 24, including Hue, The Da Vinci Cryptex and High on Life.

Steam / GOG

No separate Steam 100%-free-to-keep giveaway or notable temporary GOG giveaway was confirmed for this run. Steam's current event activity is instead concentrated around the Party-Based RPG Fest and other genre promotions.

5. LINUX APPS

1) GNOME 51

GNOME 51 is the newest major GNOME desktop release, bringing work on frame scheduling, screen capture and the modern Linux graphics stack. It is especially interesting for people who care about desktop responsiveness and recording performance because several of the changes affect everyday interaction rather than adding another large desktop feature. Distribution packaging will determine when each Linux distribution makes it available.

2) Sunshine

Sunshine is an open-source self-hosted game-streaming host that turns a PC into a low-latency streaming server for compatible clients. It is useful for sending games from a desktop to phones, handhelds and other devices without depending on a proprietary cloud-gaming service. Its Linux support and hardware-encoder integration make it particularly relevant to gaming-focused Linux setups.

3) Nuclear

Nuclear is an open-source desktop music player built around a plugin architecture and customizable interface. It supports queue-based playback, themes and multiple Linux distribution formats, making it more flexible than a simple local-folder player. Its project structure also makes it interesting to users who like experimenting with open-source media applications rather than relying entirely on large commercial streaming clients.

6. PIRACY SCENE

Denuvo lawsuit against voices38 remains the major legal story

Denuvo's parent company has filed a federal lawsuit against the anonymous person or group known publicly as voices38, alleging circumvention of Denuvo Anti-Tamper in numerous PC games. Reporting on the complaint says at least 26 games are involved and that the plaintiff is seeking damages and an injunction. The allegations have not been established as facts by a court, and the identity of the defendant remains publicly unresolved. The case is notable because it moves the dispute over game DRM from release communities and technical forums into direct litigation.

Denuvo removals continue across older and recently released games

Recent DRM tracking has recorded Denuvo being removed from multiple games, including CODE VEIN 2, Dragon's Dogma 2, Mega Man Star Force Legacy Collection and Bravely Default Flying Fairy HD Remaster. These changes are legitimate publisher updates and are separate from unauthorized circumvention activity. DRM removal later in a game's lifecycle is increasingly being used as publishers move away from launch-period protection, sometimes alongside optimization or maintenance updates.

The DRM discussion is increasingly about lifecycle policy

The current PC DRM landscape is no longer only about whether protection exists at launch. Publishers are also making decisions about how long it remains in a game, how it interacts with performance and whether it is removed once the commercial launch window has passed. At the same time, DRM vendors are pursuing stronger enforcement and legal measures around alleged circumvention. That creates a continuing tension between launch-window protection, long-term maintenance and player expectations around ownership and software longevity.

Unverified release claims remain separate from confirmed developments

Communities continue to circulate claims about very fast releases and alleged alternative approaches to protected games, but individual claims can be difficult to independently verify. A community post, a reported workaround and a complete unauthorized release are not necessarily the same thing, and authorship claims can also be wrong. For this brief, those claims are treated separately from confirmed legal filings, publisher DRM removals and independently reported industry developments.

Broader trend

The most consequential confirmed developments currently sit on both sides of the DRM lifecycle: protection remains a major launch strategy for publishers, while removals are increasingly appearing in later updates, and legal action is becoming more visible when vendors believe their protection has been deliberately circumvented. The voices38 lawsuit adds a new legal dimension to that ongoing conflict without resolving the underlying technical or commercial debate.

item.title: Daily Gaming & Tech Brief — September 18, 2026
item.description:
1. GAME & TECH NEWS

GAME NEWS

1) September 18's PC release wave is packed

Today's Steam release calendar includes a broad mix of new games, including Anymaker, Wand & Order: Tidy up the magic shop!, Sunken Realms, Nightwater, Paver: Tidy Up Together and Crown Siege. The late-September calendar then moves into larger releases such as SILENT HILL: Townfall on September 23 and CONTROL Resonant and EA SPORTS FC 27 on September 24. The consequence is a storefront where several different genres are competing for attention almost every day.

2) Active Matter joins the extraction-shooter wave

Active Matter is launching as a multiverse-themed extraction shooter, adding another science-fiction take on a genre that has become increasingly crowded. At the same time, established games such as Arena Breakout: Infinite are using large seasonal additions to retain players. That makes launch timing and differentiation increasingly important for new extraction games.

3) NASCAR 26 arrives

NASCAR 26 is part of the September 18 release wave, bringing another annual licensed racing game to PC and consoles. The PC edition is listed at $59.99, with additional seasonal content available separately. Its launch adds another established sports property to an already unusually busy September.

4) SILENT HILL: Townfall is one week from launch

SILENT HILL: Townfall is scheduled for September 23 and is listed on Steam at $49.99. The first-person horror game is one of the month's more prominent releases and lands between today's smaller launches and next week's major releases. Its placement makes the final week of September particularly crowded for horror and action-game players.

5) EA SPORTS FC 27 arrives September 24

EA lists EA SPORTS FC 27 for September 24 at $69.99. The yearly football release is arriving in the same general window as CONTROL Resonant, creating another high-profile PC release collision. The launch begins the next annual cycle of EA's licensed football series with updated squads and seasonal content.

6) Minecraft Dungeons II and other major games are approaching

Minecraft Dungeons II is currently scheduled for September 29, followed by ACE COMBAT 8 on October 1 and Phantom Blade Zero on October 28. The calendar shows that September's crowded schedule is not a short spike: October is immediately carrying the momentum forward. For players, that means wishlist management and release prioritization are becoming increasingly useful.

TECH NEWS

1) Nvidia GeForce support is appearing in SteamOS development

Valve is bringing Nvidia GeForce support into SteamOS development, although the implementation is not finished. Historically, SteamOS hardware has been dominated by AMD graphics, so broader Nvidia support could eventually make SteamOS more relevant to desktop gaming PCs. This is development work rather than a finished general-purpose Nvidia SteamOS release.

2) GNOME 51 releases with graphics improvements

GNOME 51 released this week with improved frame scheduling, smoother desktop responsiveness and faster screen capture. Mutter also adds newer Wayland support and removes legacy Nvidia EGLStreams support. The release is particularly relevant to Linux gaming and media users because frame pacing and capture performance affect everyday use.

3) Apple is reportedly considering enterprise AI servers

Reuters reports that Apple is exploring enterprise AI servers based on future Apple silicon, with Nvidia interconnect technology reportedly being considered. The project is described as long-term and could still change or be cancelled. If it ships, it would extend Apple's custom-silicon strategy into data-center inference hardware.

4) Huawei says Ascend demand exceeds supply

Huawei chairman Eric Xu says demand for the company's Ascend AI hardware in China is exceeding production capacity. Huawei is also working on larger systems that connect many processors, reflecting China's continued push for domestic AI infrastructure while access to some advanced foreign accelerators remains restricted. The development highlights how AI competition is increasingly about complete computing systems, not only individual chips.

5) SteamOS is expanding its compatibility stack

Valve's SteamOS work for Steam Frame uses more than Proton, including FEX for translating x86 software to ARM and Android compatibility technology for Android applications. SteamOS is therefore becoming a broader compatibility platform capable of handling several architectures and software ecosystems. That could matter for future SteamOS hardware as much as it does for the current device.

6) Linux graphics infrastructure continues moving toward modern APIs

GNOME 51's Mutter work, Wayland development and Valve's SteamOS changes all point toward a Linux graphics stack increasingly centered on modern APIs and compositors. For gamers, this affects frame scheduling, display handling, capture and driver support rather than simply desktop appearance. The practical impact will arrive gradually as distributions and hardware stacks adopt the new components.

2. STEAM SALE / EVENT

Steam Party-Based RPG Fest — September 14–21

Steam's current official event is Party-Based RPG Fest, running September 14 through September 21. It focuses on RPGs where players control multiple party members with different roles, equipment and abilities. The event combines discounts with demos and upcoming games, so it functions as both a sale and a discovery event.

Participating games range from established party RPGs to smaller projects and new releases. The event overlaps with the current RPG launch calendar, including Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter. Tokyo Game Show is not counted here because it is not itself a Steam promotion.

3. XODUS

Current status

Xodus remains an active open-source project focused on bringing Xbox PC and Game Pass software toward Linux and macOS execution. Its public work covers authentication, Xbox runtime compatibility, MSIXVC package handling and Wine integration.

1) Account and acquisition infrastructure: login, Xbox authorization, package downloading and license acquisition are documented as working pieces, meaning the project has moved beyond being only a launcher concept.

2) MSIXVC2: newer Microsoft package handling remains an active engineering area because modern Xbox PC games depend heavily on Microsoft's packaged distribution format.

3) Executable handling: on-demand executable decryption remains listed as unfinished work, separating successful content acquisition from broad game execution.

4) Runtime compatibility: Xbox Services and Wine-side compatibility remain major execution hurdles, with the project maintaining separate components for the runtime, authentication and patched Wine.

Progress: active development toward game execution

4. FREE GAMES

Epic Games Store

Mindcop and Shogun Showdown are the current Epic Games Store free-to-keep games for September 17–24. They remain in the Epic library after being claimed during the promotion. Mindcop is a mystery investigation game, while Shogun Showdown combines turn-based combat with roguelike and deck-building systems.

Amazon Prime / Luna

The September 17 claim wave includes DOOM Eternal via Microsoft Store code, Rims Racing via Epic Games Store and Wall World 2 via the Amazon Games App. The September 24 wave is scheduled to add Hue, The Da Vinci Cryptex and High on Life.

Steam / GOG

Steam currently has Dying Light: The Beast - Discharge Weapon Pack and Space Menace listed as free-to-keep promotions, running through September 24 and September 23 respectively. These are actual permanent claims rather than free weekends. No additional notable temporary GOG giveaway was confirmed for this run.

5. LINUX APPS

1) GNOME 51

GNOME 51 is the newest major GNOME desktop release, with frame-scheduling improvements, faster capture and newer graphics infrastructure. It is especially interesting for gaming-oriented Linux desktops because several changes target responsiveness and graphics behavior.

2) Sunshine

Sunshine is an open-source self-hosted game-streaming host that turns a PC into a low-latency streaming server for compatible clients. It is useful for sending games from a Linux desktop to handhelds, phones and other devices without relying on a proprietary cloud-gaming service.

3) Nuclear

Nuclear is an open-source music player with a plugin architecture, queue management and customizable themes. It supports Linux packaging and focuses on music discovery and streaming, making it a more unusual desktop media option than a basic local-file player.

6. PIRACY SCENE

Denuvo vs. voices38 remains the major legal development

Denuvo filed a federal lawsuit on September 14 against the anonymous figure known as voices38, alleging circumvention of Denuvo Anti-Tamper in at least 26 PC games. The complaint reportedly includes major titles such as Hogwarts Legacy, DOOM: The Dark Ages and Resident Evil Requiem, and seeks damages and an injunction. These are allegations in an ongoing case, and the defendant's identity has not been established publicly.

Official DRM removals continue

Publishers continue removing Denuvo from games later in their lifecycles, sometimes alongside maintenance and optimization updates. Those are legitimate publisher changes and are separate from unauthorized circumvention. The pattern matters because it increasingly makes DRM a lifecycle decision rather than simply a launch-time decision.

Rapid-release and bypass claims remain difficult to verify

Communities continue discussing fast releases, conventional cracks and alternative DRM bypass approaches, but individual claims about authorship, completeness or technical methods are not consistently independently verified. Confirmed legal filings and official DRM changes are therefore kept separate from community claims.

The scene is broader than one lawsuit

The current PC DRM landscape includes continued Denuvo deployment, official removals, alleged circumvention, legal enforcement and Linux compatibility issues. The voices38 lawsuit is a major current development within that wider scene, rather than the only relevant story.
